title: Designing a two-server corporate Qwen farm
summary: Part 1 of 3: size two Linux GPU inference hosts, define the application and security boundaries, and decide how a corporate chat service behaves under load and failure.
learningObjectives: Separate durable application state from disposable inference state
Estimate memory and throughput with explicit assumptions
Defend stateless API balancing and optional inference locality
Design privacy-aware provider selection and failure behavior
Decide when asynchronous infrastructure is justified

sections.title: 1. Start with the service contract
paragraphs: The target is an internal chat service with two Linux GPU machines, each running one llama.cpp server in Docker with the same Qwen GGUF. These are independent replicas: neither machine needs the other machine's GPU to answer a request. A separate control host runs Nginx, two stateless Express replicas, and PostgreSQL. This tutorial describes an educational deployment; the Windows learning application displaying it is not an inference host. No benchmark or production deployment is implied by the examples.

Define success before choosing flags. For a hypothetical department, assume 100 registered people, at most eight admitted generations across both inference hosts, an 8,192-token per-request context ceiling including output, and a 512-token output cap. Proposed service objectives might be a four-second p95 time to first token and an answer within 45 seconds for the agreed prompt distribution. These are requirements to test, not capabilities promised by any GPU. Long document ingestion and unattended batch work are separate workloads.

Express is the application boundary. It authenticates people, authorizes conversations, chooses providers, assembles prompts, assigns request identifiers, records revisions, and writes history. PostgreSQL is authoritative. Inference performs computation and may retain ephemeral KV or prefix caches. A restart may destroy that warmth without destroying a conversation. This division makes correctness independent of which API or GPU receives the next turn. The llama.cpp built-in chat UI bypasses this boundary and is therefore an operator diagnostic surface, not the corporate entry point.

sections.title: 2. Size memory before counting users
paragraphs: Use a deliberately explicit planning envelope: one 24 GiB NVIDIA GPU, 64 GiB system RAM, eight or more suitable CPU cores, and local SSD storage per inference host. This is an assumed lab shape, not a purchasing recommendation. Choose a Qwen model and quantization only after task-quality evaluation; the official Qwen guide documents GGUF operation with llama.cpp. Both hosts must share the artifact checksum, tokenizer, chat template, inference settings, and public alias corp-qwen. An identical alias alone does not establish identical model identity. [Qwen GGUF guide](https://qwen.readthedocs.io/en/v3.0/run_locally/llama.cpp.html).

A first weight estimate is parameter count multiplied by effective bits per parameter. An assumed eight-billion-parameter model at exactly four bits would use 4.0 billion bytes, approximately 3.73 GiB. Real GGUF files include metadata and mixed precision tensors, so use the actual file and runtime allocation instead of this lower-level estimate. For planning, reserve 5 GiB for loaded weights, 3 GiB for runtime and work buffers, and 4 GiB for operational headroom. Those deliberately rounded values leave 12 GiB for KV state within the assumed 24 GiB device.

For an illustrative grouped-query attention architecture with 32 layers, eight KV heads, head dimension 128, and two-byte K and V elements, cache cost is 131,072 bytes per token. Four simultaneous sequences at 8,192 tokens each need 4 GiB of raw KV storage. This is not a claim about the chosen Qwen artifact: read its actual metadata and serving allocation. Padding, cache type, attention architecture, shared prefixes, and implementation details change the result. Memory arithmetic establishes plausibility; only a maximum-context concurrency test establishes fit.
sections.formula: KV bytes ≈ 2 × layers × KV heads × head dimension × bytes/element × total cached tokens; 2 × 32 × 8 × 128 × 2 × (4 × 8192) = 4 GiB

sections.title: 3. Turn token throughput into an admission budget
paragraphs: Memory capacity and useful concurrency are different limits. Suppose a future load test measures 80 aggregate output tokens per second per host at four concurrent streams for the selected prompt mix. Two hosts would supply 160 aggregate output tokens per second. At 400 output tokens per average request, the decode-only ceiling would be 0.4 requests per second, or 24 per minute. This calculation ignores prompt processing, idle gaps, contention, and long-tail responses, so it is an optimistic ceiling rather than an admission setting.

For a rough mixed-load estimate, assume 60 percent of that decode budget remains useful after those effects. The resulting budget is 14.4 requests per minute. At a hypothetical mean residence time of 20 seconds, Little's law predicts 4.8 requests in service on average. This fits beneath eight available slots, but averages cannot prove the p95 objective. Bursty arrivals and large prompts can still exhaust all slots. Measure prompt evaluation separately from decode and record the full latency distribution at every tested concurrency.

Plan degraded service deliberately. Losing one machine halves the illustrative throughput and slot budget. A department that requires unchanged service after a failure must operate below the surviving machine's tested sustainable rate or purchase spare capacity. Otherwise, document reduced availability and return explicit 429 or 503 responses with appropriate retry guidance. Bounded admission prevents an invisible, ever-growing latency queue. Replica-local limits in the teaching API are best effort: two independent counters do not constitute a global eight-slot semaphore.
sections.formula: Decode ceiling = (2 hosts × 80 tokens/s/host) ÷ 400 tokens/request = 0.4 requests/s; L = λW = 0.24 requests/s × 20 s = 4.8 active requests

sections.title: 4. Separate API balancing from inference locality
paragraphs: Nginx uses least_conn across api1 and api2. This considers active connections, which is useful when streamed responses keep connections open for different durations. It is not a GPU-aware scheduler and does not measure tokens remaining. No sticky user routing is required because API identity and history live in PostgreSQL. A follow-up request can reach either API replica. Nginx documents the exact balancing behavior in its [upstream module reference](https://nginx.org/en/docs/http/ngx_http_upstream_module.html).

Inference placement is a separate decision inside Express. Optional rendezvous hashing scores each healthy same-model endpoint with hash(conversationId, serverId), then selects the highest score. Stable membership tends to send a conversation back to the same GPU. That can improve cache reuse, but the application must still supply the authorized prompt history on every call. Routing to the same host does not guarantee that llama.cpp retained or selects the matching cache. Never use raw bearer tokens as affinity keys or expose them in logs.

Locality competes with load distribution. Several long conversations can favor one host while the other is idle. A production scheduler can override preference when a tested queue or token budget is exceeded, recording the reason. Health failure also overrides affinity. Losing a cache increases prompt processing cost; it must not change ownership or erase history. The introductory scaffold should not be mistaken for such a cluster scheduler, and a hash should never be presented as a consistency mechanism.

sections.title: 5. Put authentication beside authorization
paragraphs: Choose Express as the application authentication owner for this example. Login exchanges the configured Admin password for an opaque server-side session stored in PostgreSQL. Requests resolve that session and then verify conversation ownership; knowing a conversation ID is insufficient. Nginx handles edge transport and can add a coarse network or enterprise access boundary. A gateway-only password gate cannot express which conversation each person may read, and two unrelated authentication systems create confusing logout and auditing behavior.

A production identity provider may authenticate at an upstream gateway, but Express must consume a verified identity through a trusted channel and still authorize each operation. Strip client-supplied identity headers at the edge. Protect cookies with Secure in HTTPS deployments, HttpOnly, suitable SameSite behavior, expiration, and explicit CSRF defenses where needed. Restrict inference ports to the control tier and keep provider credentials server-side. A single shared Admin account is a lab shortcut, not a usable corporate identity design.

Local execution is a data-routing choice, not proof of privacy. Prompts can leak through application logs, browser storage, backups, telemetry, or administrative access. Define retention and deletion for all copies. Default ALLOW_CLOUD=false. Enabling a cloud provider requires an explicit server-side policy for the user, data class, destination, and purpose; a provider button alone is insufficient. A failed local request must never silently export its transcript. Cloud training, retention, residency, and endpoint-specific controls are separate questions; review the provider's current agreement and documentation, such as [OpenAI data controls](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/your-data).

sections.title: 6. Make a turn durable without holding a transaction open
paragraphs: A turn begins with a client request ID and expected conversation revision. In a short database transaction, Express verifies ownership, checks the revision, enforces one active generation for that conversation, and records the user message plus a generation record. A unique idempotency key allows a repeated browser request to resolve to the existing operation rather than create another turn. Row locking or conditional updates serialize this acceptance decision. PostgreSQL describes row-level locking in its [explicit locking documentation](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/explicit-locking.html).

Commit before contacting inference. Holding a database connection and row lock throughout a 30-second generation makes slow GPUs a database availability problem. After committing, Express assembles the bounded prompt and streams inference output with HTTP/SSE. Streamed text is provisional until the terminal database update succeeds. Finalization records complete, error, or canceled status and advances the authoritative revision. Clients reconcile with a fresh snapshot after completion, reconnection, or a revision conflict; a stream alone is not durable history.

The gap between database acceptance and inference execution cannot be wished away. A process can crash after recording a turn but before dispatch, or after the model finishes but before storing the result. Leases and stale-generation recovery make these abandoned operations visible. A lab scaffold may recover only when later traffic performs cleanup, and may lose provisional text on a hard process crash. State those limitations. Stronger autonomous recovery requires a background worker, careful lease fencing, and a defined partial-result persistence policy.

sections.title: 7. Keep Kafka out of the first interactive path
paragraphs: The first version uses synchronous HTTP/SSE between Express and inference. Interactive users need prompt feedback, bounded waiting, cancellation, and clear failures. Kafka would add brokers, consumers, correlation, lag management, and a second channel for streamed results without increasing GPU capacity. A queue can absorb a burst by making callers wait; it cannot turn an overloaded decoder into a faster one. Choose admission limits and explicit rejection before adding durable infrastructure.

Durable asynchronous work is a different contract. A report-generation job may survive disconnects and wait minutes. Accept it with a database outbox record in the same transaction as the job, then let a worker claim work under a lease. Add idempotency, retry limits, a dead-letter policy, and per-conversation ordering. Kafka is one possible transport when event volume, replay, or multiple independent consumers justify it. Its transaction semantics do not automatically make an external LLM call and a PostgreSQL write one atomic action. [Kafka delivery-semantics discussion](https://kafka.apache.org/41/design/design/).

sections.title: 8. Define the failure matrix before enabling retries
paragraphs: A useful failure matrix states what the user sees, what PostgreSQL retains, and which component may retry. If inference A is unhealthy before dispatch, choose healthy B with the same model identity. If A fails after tokens have reached the client, end with a partial/error state; silently starting over can concatenate incompatible completions. Even before visible output, an ambiguous upstream timeout may mean compute already started, so bound any retry and preserve one logical generation identity.

If an API replica dies, Nginx can route subsequent requests to the other replica, but cannot reconstruct the dead stream. The client reconnects and reads authoritative status. If PostgreSQL is unavailable, fail closed for authentication and new durable turns; do not improvise local history. If the gateway or control host fails, both GPU machines can be healthy while the service remains unavailable. Two inference replicas do not provide database, gateway, or host high availability. Backups and restore drills are different from automated failover.

Cancellation is also a race. Browser disconnect, explicit cancel, model completion, and final database commit may overlap. Use conditional terminal updates so stale workers cannot overwrite a newer result, and abort upstream work best effort. Record the accepted terminal outcome rather than promising instant GPU reclamation. A deployment needs tested shutdown behavior: stop accepting new work, allow a bounded drain, finalize interrupted generations where possible, and let recovery identify anything left active.
bullets: Inference unavailable before dispatch → healthy same-model fallback or 503; retain one accepted operation.
Inference breaks after output → explicit partial/error; preserve what the implementation can durably retain; no silent replay.
API process dies → broken stream and later snapshot reconciliation; stale active generation requires recovery.
PostgreSQL fails → reject stateful operations; restore database service before accepting durable turns.
Gateway/control host fails → whole entry path unavailable; inference redundancy does not cover this failure.

sections.title: 9. Validate the whole path, then operate it
paragraphs: The deployment companion provides Linux Docker configuration; the routing companion explains the reference Express application and consistency behavior. Start with the example README and treat its declared limitations as part of the interface. The NVIDIA driver and Container Toolkit must be configured on each GPU host before Docker can expose the GPU. Pin a tested inference image digest, mount the selected model read-only, and record artifact checksums alongside configuration. The official [NVIDIA installation guide](https://docs.nvidia.com/datacenter/cloud-native/container-toolkit/install-guide.html) describes runtime setup.

Validation has three layers. First test GPU visibility, model loading, authenticated inference access, and a small direct completion from the control network. Then test the browser-through-gateway path: login, new conversation, streamed reply, reload, ownership rejection, duplicate request, and stale revision. Finally inject failures: terminate inference during output, restart an API, interrupt the database, cancel a request, and exceed admission capacity. Compare visible status with database history after each test. These procedures are proposed operator checks, not tests claimed to have run here.

Observe time to first token, inter-token delay, total latency, input/output token counts, admission rejection, active generations, prompt-processing time, GPU memory, and terminal outcomes. Correlate gateway, API, and inference using request IDs without logging cookies or full prompts by default. Run mixed short/long prompts and warm/cold cache cases; a single empty-context tokens-per-second number cannot validate the service objective. llama.cpp exposes serving and metrics options documented in its [server reference](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/tools/server/README.md).

For upgrades, drain one inference host, install the tested artifact and configuration, validate model identity and task quality, then restore traffic before touching the second host. During a model migration, do not label different weights as interchangeable replicas; select the intended version explicitly or maintain separate pools. Keep rollback artifacts and a database-compatible application rollback plan. The reference scaffold teaches a runnable local path; corporate SSO, distributed admission, autonomous recovery, database HA, retention enforcement, and audited cloud governance remain engineering work.

interview.question: A department wants 100 users on two 24 GiB GPU hosts, sticky sessions, Kafka, and automatic cloud fallback. How would you defend a first design?
interview.answer: Clarify arrival rate, prompt/output distribution, quality requirements and data policy instead of sizing from registered users. Use two same-model llama.cpp replicas behind an Express application that owns PostgreSQL state. Balance stateless APIs with Nginx least_conn; optional inference locality is only a cache optimization. Estimate weights and KV memory, then measure mixed-load latency and degraded one-host capacity. Start with bounded HTTP/SSE admission. Introduce durable job infrastructure only for an explicit asynchronous requirement. Default to local-only routing, require policy approval before cloud export, and never silently retry after emitted tokens. Explain that two GPUs do not make the control host or database highly available.
followUps: How would a shared admission controller avoid oversubscribing both replicas?
What must be fenced when a stale generation worker resumes?
How would you migrate conversations between model versions?
Which privacy controls apply to backups and diagnostic logs?

pitfalls: Sizing by employee count instead of arrival rates and token distributions.
Treating two model aliases as proof of identical weights and templates.
Using sticky API sessions to conceal process-local authoritative history.
Treating cache locality as a guarantee of conversation consistency.
Keeping a database transaction open while the GPU generates.
Silently exporting a transcript to cloud after a local failure.
Assuming Kafka transactions make external generation exactly once.
Calling two GPU replicas a highly available service while the control tier has one host.
checklist: Write latency, context, output and degraded-service requirements before sizing.
Record model checksum, template, quantization, runtime digest and settings for both hosts.
Measure maximum-context memory and mixed-load latency at candidate concurrency.
Keep auth, ownership, revisions and durable turns in PostgreSQL through Express.
Restrict inference network access and keep provider keys out of the browser.
Configure streaming without proxy buffering and validate cancellation behavior.
Test duplicate submissions, revision conflicts, mid-stream failures and restart recovery.
Document cloud policy, retention, backup handling and content-safe logging.
Practice restore and rollback; label reference-app limits before organizational adoption.

flashcards.front: Which component owns durable conversation state?
flashcards.back: Express writes authoritative PostgreSQL records. Inference caches are disposable, so GPU restarts must not erase history.

flashcards.front: Why do stateless Express replicas not need sticky sessions?
flashcards.back: Either replica can resolve the shared session and conversation from PostgreSQL; routing preference is unnecessary for correctness.

flashcards.front: What does least_conn measure, and what does it miss?
flashcards.back: It balances active upstream connections with weights. It does not measure GPU token work or remaining generation duration.

flashcards.front: Why use optional rendezvous hashing for inference?
flashcards.back: It can preserve conversation locality across a stable endpoint set and reduce cold prompt processing, but does not guarantee cache reuse or consistency.

flashcards.front: Why is model-file size insufficient for GPU sizing?
flashcards.back: Serving also needs KV state, work buffers and runtime overhead. Concurrent context lengths can dominate the remaining allocation.

flashcards.front: How is raw KV memory estimated for ordinary grouped-query attention?
flashcards.back: Multiply two for K and V by layers, KV heads, head dimension, bytes per element and total cached tokens; inspect actual architecture and allocation afterward.

flashcards.front: How do output tokens per second translate into a request ceiling?
flashcards.back: Divide aggregate output throughput by mean output tokens per request, then account for prompt processing and contention; this alone cannot predict tail latency.

flashcards.front: What does surviving one of two identical GPU failures imply?
flashcards.back: Remaining capacity is roughly one host's tested budget. Unchanged service requires spare capacity or a workload already below that budget.

flashcards.front: Why is a gateway password gate insufficient for chat authorization?
flashcards.back: It can restrict entry but does not establish ownership of each conversation; Express must authorize every history and mutation operation.

flashcards.front: Why must local failure not trigger silent cloud fallback?
flashcards.back: Fallback changes the data destination and privacy boundary. Server-side policy must explicitly allow transmitting that conversation.

flashcards.front: Why commit the accepted turn before inference?
flashcards.back: It preserves the request durably without tying database locks and connections to slow generation. Crash recovery must address the resulting dispatch window.

flashcards.front: Why avoid automatic retry after streamed tokens?
flashcards.back: A new generation can diverge and duplicate text already shown. Report a partial/error state and reconcile the authoritative turn.

flashcards.front: When is a durable queue justified?
flashcards.back: When work must survive disconnects, wait asynchronously, replay events or serve multiple consumers. Interactive streaming alone does not justify broker complexity.

flashcards.front: Why are two inference replicas not complete high availability?
flashcards.back: The gateway, database and control host remain separate failure domains. Their redundancy, backups and restore procedures must be designed independently.
